fix.shows: It is a documentary report by Frontline on the revision in Telangana, reported and scripted by Ayesha Minhaz. It says the state had about 3.38 crore electors when the revision began on 15 June and 2.65 crore on the draft roll of 17 August, and that nearly 73 lakh names were left off the draft as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate. It says nearly 93 lakh electors on the draft, about 35 per cent of it, received notices over logical discrepancies or because they could not be mapped to the 2002 roll, for reasons that included a small spelling mismatch, an age gap between a parent and a child judged too small, and several children mapped to the same parent. In Hyderabad's constituencies the report says many booth level officers rarely visited homes. It meets electors who say they handed in their enumeration forms and were still listed as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, electors marked permanently shifted who still live at the address on the roll, and electors marked dead without a visit. It describes Form 6 with a declaration linking the elector to the 2002 roll as the way back, Form 6 applications rejected without reasons, and the bulk Form 7 applications in at least four Hyderabad constituencies, and it says the Chief Electoral Officer has yet to disclose more than 70 per cent of the Form 7 applications filed in the state.

fix.shows: It is Amit Baruah's SpeakEasy conversation with the senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, recorded before the INDIA bloc rally of 1 November. Bhushan argues that electors who moved house were made to return through Form 6, which he says asks the applicant to declare that they have never voted before, when Form 8 for shifted electors would have kept their EPIC number. He says he would not sign such a declaration even with an assurance that no one would be prosecuted for it. He proposes that a revision be done through ward and gram sabhas at each booth, with the old roll read aloud and the meeting filmed, and says this was once done in several areas of Rajasthan. He says he suspects that the method for flagging logical discrepancies was designed to single out Muslim electors, and gives as his reason that two thirds of those flagged in West Bengal were Muslim in a state where Muslims are 27 per cent of the population. He criticises the Commission's affidavit on how the decision to hold the revision across the country was taken, and cites an RTI reply to Anjali Bhardwaj that he says shows no record of such a decision. He calls for the revision to be scrapped, the rolls from before it to be restored and the elections held on its rolls to be scrapped too, which he says he does not expect to happen. The second half of the conversation is about the youth protests, the opposition parties and the place of money in elections.

fix.shows: Frontline's Suhrid Sankar Chattopadhyay talks with Prasenjit Bose, who chairs the SIR panel of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress Committee and moved the Supreme Court after the state's Assembly election. Bose argues that Muslim electors were deleted out of proportion to their share and that the BJP would not have won its majority without the deletions. Citing figures he says the Commission gave in reply to his petition, he puts the Form 6 applications in the state at about 34 lakh, of which about 20 per cent, some 7 lakh, were accepted and about 20 lakh were still pending in August. Against that he puts about 6.3 lakh Form 7 applications, of which about 90 per cent, some 5.7 lakh, led to deletions. He says the tribunals hold about 38 lakh cases, about 22 lakh of them appeals by electors deleted after adjudication and about 16 lakh appeals against electors whom judicial officers found eligible, and that 93 per cent of the about 1.26 lakh cases decided so far went in favour of inclusion. He asks that the 22 lakh be restored before their cases are heard, so that they can vote in the coming municipal elections, that the 16 lakh appeals be cancelled, and that electors with appeals pending be allowed to apply through Form 6 as deleted electors in other states can. He says faults in the ECINET and ERONET portals are slowing the tribunals, and calls for a judicial inquiry and a forensic audit of both portals in every state where the revision has been held.
